questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that LDV performance work should be treated as an ongoing lifecycle rather than a one-time remediation project?
options: Because Salesforce requires a new performance review every time a release is pushed
Because indexes automatically expire every six months and must be re-requested

Because an org's data volume keeps growing in production, so the conditions that create LDV problems (selectivity thresholds, skew ratios, total record count) keep shifting over time even without any single change being responsible
Because Big Objects require annual re-certification by Salesforce Support
questions.explain: Data volume keeps growing every day an org is in production, which means a query that was comfortably selective or an Account with a healthy child-record count can drift toward problem territory over time with no single triggering change — hence the need for ongoing attention, not a one-time fix.

questions.q: A client reports that a specific bulk update job is failing with lock timeout errors. Per this lesson's triage framework, what should be checked first?
options: Whether the objects involved have data skew, since that's the root cause behind most lock contention
Whether the object should be converted into a Big Object
Whether the org's Recycle Bin retention window needs to be shortened
Whether a new division should be requested from Salesforce Support
questions.explain: Per the write-path triage, skew is checked first because it's the underlying cause of most record-locking contention — jumping straight to batch mode changes or Support escalation skips diagnosing the actual root cause.

questions.q: A client says the org "just feels generally slower every year" with no single query or job clearly at fault. Which category does this lesson say this complaint most likely belongs to?
options: A read-path complaint requiring a custom index
A volume-management problem, since an ever-growing, never-archived active data set makes every other tool in Chapters 1 and 2 work against a progressively larger and less selective working set
A write-path complaint requiring serial-mode batch processing
A user-interface rendering bug unrelated to data volume
questions.explain: A diffuse, generalized slowdown with no single query or job to blame is the signature of a volume-management problem — the active data set has grown without anything archiving or deleting it, making every other performance tool's job progressively harder.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say that applying a read-path fix (like requesting a custom index) to what's actually a write-path skew problem is a wasted effort?
options: Because custom indexes always make write-path problems worse, never better
Because Salesforce Support automatically rejects custom index requests tied to locking errors
Because custom indexes can only be requested once per org, ever
Because a custom index addresses query selectivity, not record-locking contention caused by skewed ownership or parent relationships — so it doesn't address the actual cause of the complaint
questions.explain: A custom index is a read-path tool aimed at query selectivity; it does nothing to address record-locking contention, which stems from data skew — misdiagnosing the category wastes the Support case without fixing the underlying problem.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what do the three chapters of this course's toolkit have in common structurally?
options: They are three interchangeable ways to solve the exact same problem, so only one needs to be learned
They only apply to orgs using Big Objects

Each addresses a distinct angle (reads, writes, active data set size) and none substitutes for the others — a well-indexed query still struggles against a skewed data model, and good batch organization still degrades if nothing ever archives or deletes data
They are listed in the order Salesforce recommends implementing them chronologically, with no other relationship
questions.explain: Chapters 1–3 address genuinely distinct angles (read performance, write reliability under concentration, and active-data-set growth) that work together rather than substituting for one another — neglecting any one of them undermines the others over time.
